transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (BrightEdge Eng Lead), Sara Gomez (BrightEdge ML Infra), Omar Hassan (BrightEdge CTO)

Summary (auto): Align on benchmark harness integration and POC success criteria.

---

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm maya from Redwood, AE on this account. we also have liam and priya from the SE team. hows everyone doing?
[00:08] Daniel Park: good, doing well. thanks for setting this up.
[00:10] Omar Hassan: hi all, busy day but excited.
[00:13] Liam O'Connor: hey team. real quick agenda — review BrightEdge workload patterns, talk through harness integration, decide streaming vs non-streaming approach, and draft success criteria + timeline. sound ok?
[00:22] Sara Gomez: yep thats good. i also want to raise network and security requirements early.

[00:31] Maya Chen: great. Daniel, can you give a quick descr of the request shapes you expect — avg tokens, payload sizes, concurrency?
[00:38] Daniel Park: sure. so we have two main flows: "summarization" — short prompts, typically 20–60 tokens input, expecting 50–150 tokens output. second is "contextual-rewrite" where we send a 2–3k token document and ask for a condensed version, those are heavier. in prod we see pulses of 150–300 rps during business hours, but steady state is more like 30–60 rps.
[01:05] Priya Nair: when you say 2–3k tokens — is that raw or after tokenization?
[01:09] Daniel Park: raw, after tokenization usually ends up a bit higher, yeah.
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: okay that helps. for the harness, we need representative scripts that match those two flows. streaming will help for the summarization flow to reduce perceived latency, but for the large documents non-streaming or chunked streaming may be better.

[01:32] Sara Gomez: can you elaborate on chunked streaming?
[01:35] Liam O'Connor: sure — basically split the 2–3k input into windows, maintain KV cache where applicable, and stream partial outputs as they're available. that reduces peak memory and latency spikes, but it's more complex from the client's side.

[01:53] Maya Chen: important note — our runtime supports prefix KV cache and partial response streaming, but the behavior depends on model variant and tokenization. sometimes the speech-to-text transcription or model name is slightly different in logs — just a heads up, we've seen auto-transcripts call the cache "K-V cash" in older exports, so ignore that noise.
[02:10] Daniel Park: ha ok noted. on the scripts side we have an existing load harness built in-house. can we reuse it? it's python-based using their internal http client.
[02:20] Priya Nair: generally yes — we provide a lightweight adapter that plugs into your driver. the adapter handles auth, streaming websocket fallback, and records per-token latencies.
[02:29] Omar Hassan: what's the effort to map our telemetry to yours? we need tracing to tie a request to our logs.
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: we support trace id pass-through — if you forward an X-Trace-Id header it'll appear in our telemetry. for the harness we'll add a correlation id in the sample scripts.

[02:48] Daniel Park: good. what's the plan for test data? we cant provide raw PII in traces, so we'll anonymize, but the distribution needs to be accurate.
[02:56] Maya Chen: totally. anonymized traces are fine; length distributions and concurrency patterns are the most important. a 1:1 semantic match isn't required.

[03:04] Liam O'Connor: for the lab run we recommend two phases: Phase A: functional correctness and small-scale latency profiling (single instance, streaming vs non-streaming). Phase B: scale tests to target throughput with synthetic drivers seeded from your traces. each phase should have its own set of success criteria.

[03:24] Sara Gomez: approx how long does each phase take?
[03:26] Liam O'Connor: Phase A can be done in 2–3 days once we have scripts. Phase B typically 4–7 days depending on iterations. given calendar setup i'd say 2-week window for the whole POC is realistic.

[03:42] Maya Chen: let's talk acceptance criteria — what does BrightEdge need to see to call it a success?
[03:47] Omar Hassan: for us the top priorities are: 95th percentile latency within 300–400ms for short summarization (streaming), throughput hitting sustained 200 rps for the short flow, and cost guidance — we want to see cost per 1M tokens estimated under the proposed config. also quality regression: outputs should match current baseline in our sampled prompts (>95% parity on automated eval).
[04:12] Daniel Park: also reliability — <0.1% error rate during the load window, and graceful fallback if a node OOMs.

[04:21] Liam O'Connor: makes sense. we'll capture those as metrics: p95 latency streaming, sustained rps, token-based cost estimate, automated eval pass rate, error rate. we'll instrument end-to-end.

[04:33] Priya Nair: note on streaming: streaming adds overhead on the client and can increase token counts slightly if framing is used. so the cost estimate will include that delta.

[04:45] Sara Gomez: about private deployment — we are leaning towards VPC peering for the POC. whats needed?
[04:51] Maya Chen: for VPC peering we need CIDR ranges, peering windows and a short list of IP allowlist. full details in our security checklist. also if you require KMS integrations for logs we can discuss HSM/KMS mappings but that tends to be later in the private deployment phase.

[05:08] Daniel Park: ok i'll coordinate with infra to get peering windows.

[05:12] Liam O'Connor: one more thing — streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for large documents: streaming can help perceived latency for the user, but for long-context the model's internal attention and KV handling may make full-response batching more efficient. for the harness we'll run both patterns: chunked streaming and batch single-call to compare.

[05:37] Maya Chen: on instrumentation, what metrics do you want in the harness outputs?
[05:41] Daniel Park: per-request latency, token counts, error codes, model variant used, and traces to link back to our app.

[05:47] Priya Nair: we'll ensure the adapter emits those fields in a CSV/JSON. we also support uploading harness telemetry to a shared S3 bucket if you prefer central analysis.

[05:57] Sara Gomez: prefer S3 upload. we already have a pipeline to consume CSVs.

[06:02] Liam O'Connor: perfect. regarding model variants — we'll recommend a smaller quantized variant for the short summarization flow and a medium accuracy variant for the long-doc flow. that'll give a cost/latency tradeoff to test.

[06:17] Daniel Park: will the adapter handle automatic fallbacks to the cheaper variant on throttling? or is that an orchestration layer thing?
[06:23] Maya Chen: we have routing policies — can do per-request fallback based on latency or capacity thresholds. for the POC we'll keep routing explicit in the harness so tests are deterministic.

[06:33] Omar Hassan: ok, timeline recap?
[06:35] Maya Chen: once we share the adapter, you plug in your scripts and traces. liam runs Phase A bench and posts results, then Phase B scale runs. target: start lab week of april 6, complete by april 17.

[06:48] Daniel Park: that works. i have a couple of micro-questions on script format — our harness is async and uses websockets for streaming. does your adapter support websockets?
[06:57] Priya Nair: yes, websockets are supported. if your client is websocket-first we'll hand you a simple shim. there may be small differences in message framing — we'll include examples.

[07:10] Sara Gomez: what about TLS mutual auth? we have mTLS in our env.
[07:14] Liam O'Connor: we can support mTLS for private deployment. for the hosted POC we usually use token-based auth in a peered routing. if mTLS is required for the lab we can enable a connector, will need certs and orchestration.

[07:30] Maya Chen: let's document that as a pre-req: brightEdge to tell us their security choice for the POC (mTLS vs token) by next tuesday.

[07:36] Omar Hassan: noted.

[07:39] Daniel Park: regarding quality evals, our baseline is an internal Rouge-ish metric plus a small human-in-the-loop spot check. can you ingest automated eval scripts?
[07:47] Priya Nair: yes, we can run your eval harness as part of the pipeline. we often run BLEU/ROUGE style metrics plus a simple LLM-based hallucination check.

[07:58] Maya Chen: ok, any blockers from the customer's side?
[08:01] Sara Gomez: item: need legal signoff for logs sharing, but infra can provide anonymized traces; that's in progress.
[08:07] Omar Hassan: also want confirmation on cost model for the POC so finance can greenlight the run.

[08:13] Liam O'Connor: we will produce a preliminary cost estimate based on your token profile and recommended variants — that'll be part of the deliverables.

[08:20] Daniel Park: great. last question: do you support client-side backpressure / throttling in the adapter? our app will apply rate limits.
[08:27] Priya Nair: adapter exposes backpressure hooks and a token-based pacing module you can enable.

[08:33] Maya Chen: wrapping up — recap of next steps and artifacts to exchange. liam will share the test plan, maya will send adapter, daniel/sara will provide traces and confirm security approach, and we aim to start lab week of april 6.
[08:48] Omar Hassan: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:50] Maya Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the lab run and a short doc with success criteria draft.
